title: Practice Passage 17: The Development of Transcontinental Railroads

passage.title: The Development of Transcontinental Railroads
passage.sub_title: Analyzing Union Pacific and Central Pacific route logistics, labor forces, mountain blasting, and economic impacts.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] In the mid-19th century, the United States was divided by vast distances, making travel between the East and West coasts slow and dangerous. [A2] The journey by stagecoach took weeks, while sailing around South America took months. [A3] To unite the nation, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act in 1862. [A4] This legislation authorized the construction of the first transcontinental railroad, a massive project that would link the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

Paragraph B

[B1] Two companies were selected to build the railroad, starting from opposite directions. [B2] The Union Pacific Railroad began construction in Omaha, Nebraska, building westward across the flat Great Plains. [B3] Meanwhile, the Central Pacific Railroad started in Sacramento, California, building eastward over the rugged Sierra Nevada mountains. [B4] The two lines would eventually meet in the middle, creating a single continuous track.

Paragraph C

[C1] The Central Pacific Railroad faced immense physical barriers immediately. [C2] Workers had to blast tunnels through solid granite peaks using gunpowder and nitroglycerin. [C3] Because of the labor shortage in California, the company hired thousands of Chinese immigrants. [C4] These Chinese workers proved highly disciplined and completed the dangerous mountain construction under extreme winter conditions.

Paragraph D

[D1] In contrast, the Union Pacific Railroad dealt with different challenges on the Great Plains. [D2] Although the flat terrain allowed faster track-laying, the company faced frequent conflicts with Native American tribes defending their territories. [D3] The Union Pacific workforce consisted mainly of Irish immigrants, Civil War veterans, and former slaves. [D4] They lived in mobile camps that moved along with the advancing tracks, earning the nickname "Hell on Wheels."

Paragraph E

[E1] Materials supply was a major logistical challenge for both companies. [E2] The Central Pacific had to ship all its iron rails, locomotives, and heavy machinery from the East Coast around South America to California, a voyage taking several months. [E3] The Union Pacific, although closer to supplies, had to transport wood for railroad ties over long distances, as the Great Plains had few trees. [E4] Managing these supply lines required careful scheduling and massive coordination.

Paragraph F

[F1] The two tracks finally met on May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah. [F2] To celebrate the completion, a symbolic golden spike was driven into the final tie. [F3] The news was transmitted instantly across the nation via telegraph, triggering widespread celebrations in major cities. [F4] The completed railroad reduced travel time across the continent from months to just under one week.

Paragraph G

[G1] The transcontinental railroad had a profound impact on the nation's economy and society. [G2] It accelerated the settlement of the West, stimulated trade, and allowed businesses to ship goods nationwide. [G3] However, it also led to the rapid decline of Native American populations and the destruction of bison herds. [G4] Despite these negative consequences, the railroad remains one of the greatest engineering feats in history.
